doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Rhythm section changing the arrangement; moving to straight time
summary: Purdie describes multiple guitarists such as Vinnie Bell, the drummer out front like Gene Krupa, and asking the arranger for five minutes to alter rhythms toward straight eighths.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: you’ve got this rhythm section going and you start to create this sound. Something happens. Now you’ve got these three guitars. One is playing the backbeat (scats) and you’ve got rhythm (scats) and then you’ve got the other one might be a twang, it might be a thing with Vinnie Bell sound, water sound or a fish or a tree, a whistle. He had all kinds of little sound effects that he did. And this started to become part of the sound to go with the hook of what is happening, the thing that’s going to be repeated over and over and over again. Well that’s how things start to happen. Now for me, I was one of the lucky people. When I was coming along I never believed that the drummer had to be in the background. The drummer did not have to be in the background. Now Gene Krupa helped us. Gene Krupa was one of the first persons to bring us out front so people could see the drums. So I always felt that way because that’s how I was taught when I was coming along. Yes I was taught to play, keep my time. But I was also trying to make the drums outstanding, to be remembered. And that’s how things got with me, which is also why I had some problems with some of the music that was going down, and I was calling it old fashioned. At that particular time people like Bucky and Vinnie Bell and other folks, Bob Bushnell who actually played the Fender bass not the upright, just the upright sound, was coming into play. And it happened to come into what I liked, the kind of things that I did and something that I heard. So it was like wow, this is phenomenal. I’m not the only one that’s hearing things. New thing. Different things. You don’t have to play [scats]. You can play [scats] play it straight. Or you can play [scats] and really play it straight and come out with something that was a little bit different than [scats]. So ooh, I liked this. But still remembering what we were in there for, from what the producer wanted, the sound that the producer wanted to make this thing happen. I said okay, okay, all right, let’s go, let’s go with this. We tried something and the producer, you see the people, the horn players and the string players, they got lines and stuff that’s going on that was happening and then we would ask, well mainly I would ask, if the string players and the horn players don’t play for a minute. Give us five minutes to see if this rhythm is going to fit and maybe, just maybe the arranger might change the rhythm of what he wrote. Still get his figures, but change the rhythm slightly to make it go different and with a dotted feel. Well that was me a lot. That was part of my mouth situation. Well they would give us five minutes. We’d never get more than that, because time is money. We would try some of these things and sure enough these kind of things would happen. Your body started doing this and the arranger, especially if he’s a smart one and really good one, if he starts, he says okay — so you don’t want to go with the dotteds — okay — let’s kind of play this a little bit more straight you know. But he could tell the musicians how to play what he wanted. It was his job.
So you’re talking about transitioning the music really from more of a swing thing into straight eighth notes.
